title: A Rigid, Sterile Look at Kissing
summary: Josh and Chuck open with October wrap-up banter, then take a clinical, tongue-in-cheek look at kissing. They cover evolutionary theories (mother pre-chewing food, learned behavior vs. instinct), kissing in animals (tigers, snails, birds, bonobos), the Kinsey Institute's biological/psychological/social factors, early history from Vedic texts and the Kama Sutra, Roman kiss types, the Holy Kiss and the Protestant Reformation, facial muscles and head tilt, neurochemistry (dopamine, serotonin, oxytocin, adrenaline), a dubious claim about immune compatibility and smell, recent surveys on attraction and kissing among English heterosexual males, and diseases spread by kissing. The episode closes with a listener email from Sarah about healthy jealousy.

segments.title: Opening banter and October recap
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about kissing as the show's recurring theme, recap a busy October including TV appearances and a trip to New York, and introduce the clinical topic of kissing and the term philematology.

segments.title: Evolutionary theories of kissing
segments.summary: They discuss the theory that kissing evolved from mothers pre-chewing food for infants, and the flaw that some indigenous cultures still do this without kissing.

segments.title: Animal kissing and instinct
segments.summary: They argue for an instinctive origin, citing tigers nuzzling, snails touching antennae, birds touching beaks, and scent glands. Bonobos are described as kissing to reduce tension, build bonds, and for no reason.

segments.title: Cultures that do not kiss
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck note that around ten percent of cultures may not kiss, possibly in parts of Asia, South America, and Africa, though the evidence is inconclusive, and conclude that most cultures do kiss.

segments.title: Biological, psychological and social factors
segments.summary: The Kinsey Institute's three factors of a kiss are described: biological, psychological and social. Each affects the experience of any kind of kiss, including a mother kissing a child's boo-boo.

segments.title: Ancient history: Vedic texts, Kama Sutra, Alexander the Great
segments.summary: The earliest accounts of kissing appear in ancient Vedic Sanskrit texts from India. The Kama Sutra, standardized in the sixth century AD after oral transmission, covers kisses. They speculate Alexander the Great brought kissing from India to Greece.

segments.title: Roman kisses, Holy Kiss and the Reformation
segments.summary: Romans used greetings and three kiss types (osculum, basium, and savium). Roman kissing traditions such as the wedding kiss are thought to have originated there, and legal documents were sealed with kisses. The Holy Kiss in the Catholic Church was later replaced by the pax board and then ended by Protestants.

segments.title: Facial muscles, head tilt and tongue
segments.summary: Muscles used in kissing include the orbicularis oris, depressor anguli oris, and tongue muscles. About two-thirds of people tilt their heads to the right, possibly developed in utero. The tongue's malleability is discussed, and Josh describes seeing a removed tongue at the Hiroshima museum.

segments.title: Neurochemistry and body response to kissing
segments.summary: Kissing stimulates nerves that release dopamine, serotonin and oxytocin, linked to affection and attachment. Adrenaline and endorphins raise heart rate and blood flow even when lying down.

segments.title: Immune compatibility and smell claim
segments.summary: A claim that people can sniff out compatible immune systems through kissing is questioned, since it relies on pheromones and a vomeronasal organ that most humans no longer use. Josh notes the appendix is thought to have a function.

segments.title: Recent kissing surveys and attraction
segments.summary: A University of Albany study found many people lose attraction after the first kiss. The same professor theorizes testosterone in saliva drives sloppy kissing. A UK study found heterosexual male athletes kiss other men without concern.

segments.title: Diseases spread by kissing
segments.summary: Mono, herpes simplex one (cold sores), meningitis, the bacteria linked to gastric ulcers, and one CDC-recognized case of HIV transmitted by kissing are covered.

segments.title: Listener mail: healthy jealousy
segments.summary: Sarah writes that a small amount of jealousy is normal and healthy. Josh agrees, and Chuck is persuaded. They discuss playful PDA and whether a twinge of jealousy differs from fear of losing a partner.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: Josh invites listeners to search for kissing on HowStuffWorks and to send thoughtful emails. The episode closes with a promotional note about the iPhone app and iTunes.
